questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Detection probability in a count record
questions.learningObjective: Explain how detection probability limits a count-based estimate
questions.stem: An architect's survey of a listed building counts roof tiles from the street, and the brief must explain what that count can support.

options.text: The count is complete, because every tile on the roof is visible from the street on a clear day
options.misconception: assumes full visibility of the whole roof

options.text: The count is only of visible tiles, so it cannot give the true number without a detection estimate
The count is complete, because tiles are a regular pattern and so are easy to extrapolate
options.misconception: assumes a regular pattern removes the need for detection

options.text: The count is useless, because no tile count from the street can ever be useful
options.misconception: overstates the limitation of visual survey

questions.explanation: A street view counts only the tiles that can be seen, and obstructions hide more, so the tally is an index rather than a total. Estimating detection converts it into a number.
questions.hint: Count what you can see, not what is there.

questions.topic: Intensity of energy against a fall in output
questions.learningObjective: Interpret energy intensity when output falls
questions.stem: A building's annual energy use falls from 420 to 300 gigajoules after a refurbishment while floor area stays at 5000 square metres, and the architect must interpret the pair.

options.text: Energy intensity rose, because a smaller total over the same area is a worse performance
options.misconception: reads a lower total as worse performance

options.text: Energy intensity is unchanged, because the floor area did not change either
options.misconception: assumes unchanged area means unchanged intensity

options.text: Energy intensity fell from 0.084 to 0.06 gigajoules per square metre, so performance improved
Energy intensity fell only because the building was partly closed during the year
options.misconception: invents an occupancy cause for the reduction

questions.explanation: Intensity is energy divided by area, so 420 over 5000 is 0.084 and 300 over 5000 is 0.06. Falling intensity with unchanged area is the sign of a real improvement in the fabric.
questions.hint: Divide the energy by the floor area.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A response that begins before the intervention
questions.learningObjective: Design a study that accounts for a response that precedes the intervention
questions.stem: Occupants report lower heating bills from the year before the insulation was installed, and the architect must design a study that can separate the causes.

answer.exemplar: Collect at least two full years of bills and consumption data before the works and two years after, from the treated building and from an identical building that received no work, and normalise both for the degree days of each period and for occupancy. With a before period in which the change already appears, the pre-intervention trend can be projected forward and compared with the post-intervention record, and any programme effect measured as the difference between the two projections. Occupancy data and controls for internal heat sources must be recorded for the same reason.

questions.explanation: A pre-intervention trend must be estimated and projected forward, and that projection is the counterfactual for the treated building. Without it, the earlier fall would be credited to the works.
questions.hint: Project the old trend forward before crediting the new.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A step inside a step
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two step changes combine in a record
questions.stem: A heating record shows a drop at one date and a further drop a year later, and the architect must explain the pattern for the brief.

answer.exemplar: Two separate interventions each produce their own step, so the record contains a step within a step rather than one continuous trend. The size of each step is the change in level attributable to that intervention, and it can only be read off if the level between the two dates is used as the baseline for the second. Treating the two as a single trend hides the fact that two things changed, and leads to a saving figure that wrongly credits the later work with the earlier improvement as well.

questions.explanation: Two interventions each produce their own step, so the record holds one step inside another. The second is measured from the level after the first, not from the original line.
questions.hint: Measure the second step from the new baseline.

questions.explanation: A warm year reduces heating demand, so part of the fall is weather rather than the measures. Normalising for degree days and reporting the corrected figure makes the comparison usable.

options.misconception: assumes one visit counts for full coverage

options.text: The two counts should agree, because the defects do not change between the two checks

The floor count is higher because the scaffold obstructed the light on the wall
options.misconception: invents a lighting cause instead of access

questions.explanation: Detection depends on access and viewing angle, so a close inspection finds defects a distant one cannot. The counts measure effort as well as condition, which is why they cannot be compared directly.

options.text: The study supports the capacity estimate, because three years of gauging is a standard record length
options.misconception: treats record length as enough without checking the years

options.text: The study shows the reservoir will silt up quickly, because the measured yield is a minimum
options.misconception: reaches a firm conclusion the data cannot support

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A flow record after a channel change
questions.learningObjective: Design a survey to attribute a flow record change to a channel modification
questions.stem: A channel has been reconfigured and the downstream flow record has changed, and the architect must design a check that can attribute the change.

answer.exemplar: Extend the gauging to a pair of stations, one upstream of the works and one downstream, and run both continuously through the change so that the upstream record supplies the baseline for the same period. Extend the pre-works record far enough back to show the normal relationship between the two stations, and add a second downstream station further along so that any sediment or roughness change can be separated from a change in the channel itself. Survey the new cross sections and the bed material, and record any works or abstractions in the reach between the stations.

questions.explanation: An upstream station supplies the baseline for the same period, so a change downstream is separated from a change in the catchment. A bed survey separates the channel change from roughness.
questions.hint: You need a baseline station upstream of the works.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A response that begins before the intervention
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a pre-intervention trend changes the attribution of a saving
questions.stem: An office's electricity use fell in the year before a lighting upgrade was installed, and the architect must explain what that means for the claimed saving.

answer.exemplar: A fall that began before the upgrade cannot have been caused by it, so the pre-intervention series has to be used to establish the trend against which any saving is judged. Projecting that trend forward gives the level the building would have reached without the work, and the saving is the difference between that projection and the measured post-upgrade use. Quoting the whole fall from the start of the record as the saving of the project credits the upgrade with a change that the building was already making, which is the most common way a saving figure is overstated.

questions.explanation: A fall that began before the upgrade cannot be its doing, so the pre-intervention trend must be projected forward. Quoting the whole fall credits the project with a change it did not cause.
questions.hint: Only the change above the old trend is yours.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A flow record after a channel change
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a flow record changes after a channel modification
questions.stem: A downstream flow record rises by about a fifth after a channel was reconfigured upstream, and the architect must explain the record.

answer.exemplar: A wider, smoother channel conveys more of the same rainfall for a given slope and depth, so the rating of the downstream section changes even though the catchment inputs have not. The flow record therefore measures the new geometry rather than more water in the catchment, and any analysis that treats the rise as a hydrological change is reading the wrong signal. Re-rating the gauging section after the works and re-deriving the discharge series with the new rating is what makes the record usable again, and the pre-works series should be preserved for comparison.

questions.explanation: A wider, smoother channel conveys more for the same inputs, so the downstream rating changes even though the catchment has not. The record measures new geometry and needs re-rating.
questions.hint: The channel itself now behaves differently.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mass removed by a treatment upgrade
questions.learningObjective: Design a trial to measure the mass removed by a treatment upgrade
questions.stem: A treatment upgrade is proposed for a small works, and the architect must design a trial that shows how much mass it actually removes.

answer.exemplar: Run the existing plant and the upgraded arrangement in parallel on the same influent for a defined trial period, metering the flow and sampling the influent and effluent at matching intervals so that the concentrations are directly comparable. Weigh or calibrate the sludge removed from each line and record its solids concentration, because sludge volume alone does not give the mass. Repeat the trial across a range of influent loads, since capture efficiency that holds at one load may fall away at another, and report the whole range rather than a single figure.

questions.explanation: Running both arrangements on the same influent isolates the upgrade, and matching flow and concentration samples allow a mass balance to be closed. Repeating across loads shows whether the gain holds.

questions.topic: Sediment yield and reservoir capacity
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reservoir sediment reduces its useful capacity
questions.stem: A new dam is built on an eroding catchment, and the architect must explain what happens to the water storage over time.

answer.exemplar: Every year the reservoir traps the sediment that the catchment delivers, and that material occupies storage that the dam was built to provide, so the usable volume falls steadily from the day the scheme opens. The rate of loss depends on the catchment yield and on how much sediment the reservoir can trap rather than pass, and where it settles, near the inlet, it is most damaging because it blocks the deepest and most valuable part of the storage. The life of the scheme is therefore a moving calculation that has to be revisited as the catchment changes.

questions.explanation: Trapped sediment occupies storage the dam was built to provide, so usable volume falls from the outset. Where it settles near the inlet matters most, since that blocks the deepest part of the storage.
questions.hint: The sediment takes up room that was meant for water.

questions.topic: Mass removed by a treatment upgrade
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a treatment upgrade changes the mass removed by a plant
questions.stem: A wastewater plant is upgraded with a new tertiary stage, and the architect must explain the change for the brief.

answer.exemplar: The existing stages remove a fixed share of what arrives, so each one works on the solids that the earlier stages have already taken out. A new tertiary stage is therefore presented with a much smaller and more dilute stream than the raw influent, and the mass it removes can be far smaller than the stage's share of the original load suggests. The upgrade has to be described in terms of the mass it actually removes and the extra tonnes of sludge it produces, because the extra sludge volume determines the space, the tanker movements and the disposal cost that follow from the scheme.

questions.explanation: A later stage works on a smaller and more dilute stream than the raw influent, so its share of the original load is small even when its efficiency is high. Report the extra mass and sludge.

questions.topic: Intensity of energy against a fall in output
questions.learningObjective: Explain why energy intensity tells a different story from total consumption
questions.stem: Two buildings have the same annual energy use, and the architect must explain why the larger one is usually the better building.

answer.exemplar: Total consumption mixes the performance of the fabric with the size of the job the building is doing, so a large building with many occupants and a lot of equipment will always use more energy than a small one. Intensity divides that total by an output measure that reflects how much the building was actually used, so two buildings of very different size can be compared on the same terms. When the output measure is chosen carefully, intensity is the figure that separates a building that got more efficient from one that simply got bigger or busier, which is why it is the number quoted in comparative assessments.

questions.explanation: Total consumption mixes fabric performance with how much the building was used, so a bigger building always uses more. Intensity divides by an output measure, comparing different sizes fairly.

options.text: The new section is both wider and deeper, so both changes add to the conveyance
The diagram shows no change, because all three stations have the same design shape
options.misconception: treats a repeated shape as an unchanged section

questions.explanation: Conveyance depends on the whole section, and the diagram shows a wider and deeper channel at each station, so the capacity gain comes from both. Treating one dimension alone understates it.
questions.hint: Read both dimensions on the new section.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A response that begins before the intervention
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an error in a saving claim that ignores a pre-intervention change
questions.stem: A claim credits a new heat pump with a 25 per cent fall in gas use, and the architect must find the error.

options.text: The error is that gas and electricity savings should never be reported in the same claim
options.misconception: objects to the presentation rather than the reasoning

options.text: The error is that a heat pump saving should be measured in kilowatt hours rather than in kilowatt hours of gas
options.misconception: creates a meaningless unit distinction

options.text: The error is that the claim should be checked against the original design rather than the old building
options.misconception: redirects the error to a different comparison

options.text: The error is that the baseline year already included a change in occupancy or operation

questions.explanation: A falling baseline before the heat pump was installed means part of the fall belongs to the earlier change, so the claim takes credit for a saving already under way. The baseline is not like for like.
questions.hint: Look at what the baseline year already contained.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A step inside a step
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the combined effect of two sequential step changes
questions.stem: A record falls by 20 per cent at one date and by a further 25 per cent on the lower level a year later, and the architect must calculate the total percentage fall from the original level.
questions.explanation: After the first step the level is at 80 per cent of the original and after the second at 0.8 times 0.75, which is 0.6, so the total fall is 40 per cent. Adding the two percentages would overstate it.
questions.hint: Multiply the fractions that remain.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Weather normalisation of a demand record
questions.learningObjective: Design a weather normalisation procedure for a demand record
questions.stem: A client's energy data must be weather normalised before it supports a design decision, and the method must be defensible.

answer.exemplar: Obtain hourly or daily demand data for each year together with degree days computed from a weather station close to the site, and fit a regression of demand on degree days over the baseline years, separately for heating and for cooling where both apply. Apply the fitted relationship to convert each year's actual weather into a common reference year, then report the normalised series alongside the raw one so a reader can see how much of the movement was weather. Check the fit on a held-back year, and record any change of occupancy or plant that would break the relationship.

questions.explanation: Fitting demand against degree days over the baseline years gives a conversion to a common weather, and reporting raw and normalised series shows how much was weather. A held-back year checks it.
questions.hint: Fit demand against degree days over the baseline.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Detection probability in a count record
questions.learningObjective: Assess a fabric survey note for its treatment of detection

stimulus.body: The note reports that 240 defects were recorded across the elevations inspected from ground level, that the north elevation was inspected from a mobile platform but the south elevation could not be reached at all, and that 30 of the defects recorded on the north elevation were also visible from the ground.

questions.stem: A fabric condition note is used to price repairs, and the architect must judge what the note supports.

options.text: The note mixes viewpoints and an uninspected elevation, so the count cannot stand as a condition figure
The note is sound, because 240 defects is a large enough sample to be reliable on its own
options.misconception: treats a raw count as representative without effort data

options.text: The note is sound, because the 30 repeat defects show that the survey was thorough
options.misconception: reads repeat observations as proof of thoroughness

options.text: The note is wrong, because the south elevation was inspected from a scaffold in the previous year
options.misconception: invents a previous year survey the note does not mention

questions.explanation: Different viewpoints detect different things and the uninspected elevation is unknown, so the 240 figure mixes detection levels and gaps. The note records what was seen, not the whole building.
questions.hint: What did the survey not look at?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Intensity of energy against a fall in output
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fall in energy use differs from a fall in energy intensity
questions.stem: A building's energy use falls and its energy intensity also falls, and the architect must describe what that combination shows.

options.text: The fall in use came from reduced occupancy, because total use always tracks the number of people
options.misconception: assumes occupancy is the only possible cause

options.text: The building is doing more with less energy, so the improvement survives any change in use
The figures cannot both fall, because intensity is calculated directly from the total
options.misconception: forgets that intensity also divides by output

options.text: The fall in use is all that can be claimed, because intensity figures are not used in practice
options.misconception: dismisses a standard comparison metric

questions.explanation: When both the total and the intensity fall, the building is doing more with less energy, so the gain is not simply a consequence of being less busy. That combination carries a performance claim.
questions.hint: Both figures fell, so what does that show?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mass removed by a treatment upgrade
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a mass balance for a plant before and after an upgrade
questions.stem: A plant's influent load is 2.4 tonnes of solids a day, rising to 3.0 tonnes a day, while the mass removed rises from 2.0 to 2.85 tonnes a day, and the architect must interpret the pair.

options.text: Efficiency fell, because the mass removed rose by less than the load
options.misconception: compares absolute changes rather than ratios

options.text: Efficiency is unchanged, because more mass is removed in both cases
options.misconception: ignores the ratio when both quantities rise

options.text: Efficiency rose from about 83 to 95 per cent, so the upgrade works better
Efficiency cannot be calculated, because the influent load is not a measured quantity
options.misconception: denies that an influent load can be measured

questions.explanation: Before the upgrade the plant removed 2.0 of 2.4 tonnes, about 83 per cent, and after it removes 2.85 of 3.0 tonnes, about 95 per cent. The efficiency gain is larger than the mass rise suggests.
questions.hint: Divide the mass removed by the load arriving.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Sediment yield and reservoir capacity
questions.learningObjective: Review a reservoir life estimate for what it assumes

stimulus.body: The note states that the reservoir will deliver its design storage for 100 years at the current rate of sediment yield, that the yield figure comes from a single year of monitoring at the downstream gauge, and that it assumes the upstream land management will remain unchanged over the period.

questions.stem: A reservoir life estimate underpins a funding application, and the architect must judge the assumptions behind it.

options.text: The note is sound, because a 100 year appraisal period is a standard requirement
options.misconception: treats the appraisal length as proof the estimate is sound

options.text: The note is unsound, because no reservoir can be designed on a single year of monitoring
options.misconception: states a false general rule about monitoring periods

options.text: The note is unsound, because sediment yield must be measured at the dam rather than downstream
options.misconception: relocates the measurement without fixing the real weakness

options.text: The note is weak, because one year of yield and fixed land management are optimistic assumptions

questions.explanation: A single year of yield is unlikely to be a long term average, and assuming upstream land management never changes is optimistic because erosion responds to management. Both push the life estimate up.
questions.hint: What does the note take for granted?
